correctness.rationale: Fourier orthogonality gives exact normal eigenvalues q times the number of null projective directions perpendicular to each frequency. The anisotropic orthogonal hyperplane is nonsingular of dimension d-1, while the isotropic one has a one-dimensional radical and a d-2 dimensional nondegenerate quotient with the correct Witt sign. The quadratic Gauss-sum counts yield every eigenvalue and its multiplicity; direct inequalities prove injectivity for d>=4 and exact dimension-three kernel. Orthogonal-group transitivity proves no nonnegative per-direction scalar weighting improves the sharp condition number. Direct full-frequency enumerations over F3, F5, F9, and Gram diagonalization in two sample cases passed. The script is finite corroboration, not an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Bounded comparisons found no stated theorem of the same affine null-line measurement operator with exact Witt-dependent normal spectrum and sharp direction-weighting barrier. Koh (2012) proves unrestricted finite-field X-ray endpoint bounds, while Feldman–Grinberg (2017) solve a projective-line-complex admissibility problem. The closest public scalar-view stability statement concerns cyclic square grids, not quadratic isotropic-direction families. General quadratic zero counts and line-sum Fourier diagonalization are prior ingredients explicitly credited; any unlocated general formulation that specializes to all claimed conclusions remains a priority risk.

value.rationale: Null-direction restriction is a geometrically natural limited-view X-ray acquisition scheme; its injectivity and numerical stability are genuine inverse-problem quantities. The theorem determines the complete ambient Fourier spectrum, sharp missing information in dimension three, distinct q versus sqrt(q) instability in elliptic versus split four-dimensional geometries, and a no-remedy result for all nonnegative per-direction reweightings. These distinctions have a clear reconstruction interpretation and cannot be inferred from correctness or code alone.
